lead: A thin plate can carry load in two ways at once. Lateral pressure q bends it, and in-plane forces N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> and N<sub>xy</sub> stretch or squeeze its mid-surface. Both enter one equilibrium equation, so bending and membrane action combine. Fuselage skin feels cabin pressure as q and fuselage bending as in-plane compression; a wing skin feels fuel pressure and wing bending. Compression makes the same pressure bend the plate further, and the ratio of the applied compression to the buckling load tells you by how much.
prereq: You need: the moment–curvature relations and the plate stiffness D from pure bending of thin plates.

sections.h3: The plate equation with lateral load and membrane forces

blocks.text: Cut a small element dx × dy from a plate loaded by a pressure q (N/m²) on its face. Besides the moments M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub> and M<sub>xy</sub> it carries transverse shear forces Q<sub>x</sub> and Q<sub>y</sub> per unit length. Moment equilibrium of the element gives Q<sub>x</sub> = ∂M<sub>x</sub>/∂x + ∂M<sub>xy</sub>/∂y and Q<sub>y</sub> = ∂M<sub>y</sub>/∂y + ∂M<sub>xy</sub>/∂x; force equilibrium normal to the plate gives ∂Q<sub>x</sub>/∂x + ∂Q<sub>y</sub>/∂y + q = 0. Putting in the moment–curvature relations collapses the three equations into one, D∇⁴w = q.

Now let in-plane forces act as well. While the plate is flat they have no component normal to it. Once it bends, N<sub>x</sub> on the two faces of the element points along slightly different slopes, ∂w/∂x and ∂w/∂x + (∂²w/∂x²)dx, and leaves a net normal force N<sub>x</sub>(∂²w/∂x²)dx dy. N<sub>y</sub> and the shear N<sub>xy</sub> do the same. These act like extra pressure:

blocks.where: w is the deflection (m); D the plate stiffness (N·m); q the lateral pressure (N/m²); N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> the in-plane direct forces per unit length (N/m), tension positive; N<sub>xy</sub> the in-plane shear force per unit length (N/m); ∇⁴w = ∂⁴w/∂x⁴ + 2∂⁴w/∂x²∂y² + ∂⁴w/∂y⁴.

blocks.text: With no in-plane force the right side is just q. N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> and N<sub>xy</sub> are stress resultants, not stresses: σ<sub>x</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>/t, σ<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>y</sub>/t and τ<sub>xy</sub> = N<sub>xy</sub>/t. A compressive N<sub>x</sub> is negative. In a sagging plate ∂²w/∂x² is negative, so a negative N<sub>x</sub> adds to q: compression pushes the plate further the way it is already bent, and tension pulls it back towards flat.

sections.h3: Navier and Levy solutions and the edge conditions

blocks.text: Navier's method solves a rectangular plate a × b simply supported on all four edges. Write both the load and the deflection as double sine series, w = ΣΣ A<sub>mn</sub> sin(mπx/a) sin(nπy/b). Every term has w = 0 and zero bending moment on all four edges, so each edge condition is met term by term. For uniform pressure, the load coefficients are 16q/(π²mn) for odd m and n and zero for even ones, and:
A<sub>mn</sub> = 16q/[π⁶ D m n (m²/a² + n²/b²)²],   m, n = 1, 3, 5, …
blocks.where: A<sub>mn</sub> is the amplitude of the (m, n) term (m); a and b are the plate sides (m); m and n count half-waves along x and y.

blocks.text: The first term alone gives 4.15 mm for the plate of the worked example, 2.4% above the full sum: the series converges fast for deflection, more slowly for moments. Summing it for a square plate gives the table values w<sub>max</sub> = 0.00406 q a⁴/D and M<sub>x</sub> = M<sub>y</sub> = 0.0479 q a² at the centre for ν = 0.3. The deflection coefficient does not depend on ν, because ν is already inside D; the moment coefficient does.

Levy's method needs only two opposite edges simply supported. It expands w in a single sine series along those edges and solves an ordinary differential equation across the plate for each term, so the other two edges can be clamped or free. The edge conditions are:

head: Edge
Deflection
Second condition
rows: bending moment normal to the edge = 0
bending moment normal to the edge = 0 and effective shear V<sub>x</sub> = Q<sub>x</sub> + ∂M<sub>xy</sub>/∂y = 0; the twisting moment itself is not zero

blocks.text: For a simply supported plate under a uniform compression N<sub>x</sub> = −N, substituting the sine series into the full equation gives each term exactly:
A<sub>mn</sub>(N) = A<sub>mn</sub>(0)/(1 − N/N<sub>mn</sub>),   N<sub>mn</sub> = π²D(m²/a² + n²/b²)²/(m/a)²
blocks.where: A<sub>mn</sub>(0) is the amplitude without compression; N is the compressive force per unit length (N/m); N<sub>mn</sub> is the compression at which the (m, n) shape would stand without any pressure: its buckling load.

blocks.text: The lowest N<sub>mn</sub> is the buckling load N<sub>cr</sub> of the next chapter. Near it the first term dominates, so the deflection is magnified by about 1/(1 − N/N<sub>cr</sub>). Tension does the reverse: N enters with the other sign and the factor becomes 1/(1 + N/N<sub>mn</sub>). Small deflections add linearly; once w is comparable with t the mid-surface stretches and membrane forces grow with w, which needs large-deflection theory.

In an aircraft, cabin pressure is q and fuselage or wing bending supplies N<sub>x</sub> and N<sub>y</sub>; skins also carry N<sub>xy</sub> from shear. A compression of 0.4N<sub>cr</sub> may be safe for strength, yet it already raises the pressure deflection and bending stress by two thirds. Check both stress and stability.

figure.caption: The worked example's square plate under 1 kPa, deflection along its centre line from the Navier series. With no in-plane load the centre deflects 4.06 mm; 10 kN/m of compression (N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub> = 0.395) raises it to 6.76 mm, and 10 kN/m of tension lowers it to 2.89 mm.

spec.aria: A graph of deflection w in millimetres, drawn downward, against x from 0 to 800 millimetres along the centre line of the plate. Three sine-like curves start and end at zero. The middle one, with no in-plane load, reaches 4.06 millimetres at the centre. The deepest, with 10 kilonewtons per metre compression, reaches 6.76 millimetres. The shallowest, with 10 kilonewtons per metre tension, reaches 2.89 millimetres.

examples.question: A square plate 800 mm × 800 mm × 4 mm is simply supported on all edges, with E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.30, and carries a lateral pressure of 1 kPa. (a) Find D, the centre deflection and the centre bending moment and stress. (b) A compression N<sub>x</sub> = 10 kN/m is added on two opposite edges. Find N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub>, the single-term magnified deflection and the exact series value. (c) What would a tension of 10 kN/m do instead?
steps: Centre deflection: q a⁴/D = 1000 × 0.8⁴/410.3 = 409.6/410.3 = 0.9984 m, so w<sub>max</sub> = 0.00406 × 0.9984 = 4.05 mm. Summing the Navier series directly gives 4.06 mm (coefficient 0.00406).
Centre moment: M<sub>x</sub> = 0.0479 q a² = 0.0479 × 1000 × 0.64 = 30.7 N·m/m (series 30.6). Face stress σ = 6M<sub>x</sub>/t² = 6 × 30.6/(1.6 × 10⁻⁵) = 11.5 MPa.
Buckling load of the square plate (m = n = 1): N<sub>cr</sub> = 4π²D/b² = 4 × 9.870 × 410.3/0.64 = 25,307 N/m = 25.3 kN/m. N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub> = 10/25.3 = 0.395.

Exact series with each term divided by its own (1 − N/N<sub>mn</sub>): w = 6.76 mm, a factor 1.667. The higher terms have much larger N<sub>mn</sub>, so they are hardly magnified; the single-term estimate is within 0.8%.
Tension of 10 kN/m: the first term is divided by 1 + 0.395 instead, and the series gives w = 2.89 mm, 29% less than with no in-plane force.
examples.answer: D = 410.3 N·m; w<sub>max</sub> = 4.06 mm, M<sub>x</sub> = 30.6 N·m/m, σ = 11.5 MPa. With 10 kN/m compression N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub> = 0.395 and w ≈ 6.7 mm (6.76 mm exactly); with 10 kN/m tension w = 2.89 mm.

traps: Entering a compressive N<sub>x</sub> as a positive number in D∇⁴w = q + N<sub>x</sub> ∂²w/∂x² + …; tension is positive there, and a wrong sign makes compression appear to stiffen the plate.
Treating N<sub>x</sub> as a stress. N<sub>x</sub> is a force per unit length (N/m); σ<sub>x</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>/t.
Using the coefficient 0.00406 for clamped edges or for a non-square plate. It is for a square plate simply supported on all edges under uniform pressure.
Setting the twisting moment to zero on a free edge. The two free-edge conditions are zero bending moment and zero effective shear Q<sub>x</sub> + ∂M<sub>xy</sub>/∂y.
Checking only stress and ignoring N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub>. A compression well below yield can still magnify deflection and bending stress, and buckles the skin at N<sub>cr</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the governing equation of a thin plate under lateral pressure and in-plane forces, and state the sign convention for N<sub>x</sub>.
quiz.a: D∇⁴w = q + N<sub>x</sub> ∂²w/∂x² + 2N<sub>xy</sub> ∂²w/∂x∂y + N<sub>y</sub> ∂²w/∂y², with N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> positive in tension.

quiz.q: Which edge conditions does each term of Navier's double sine series satisfy?
quiz.a: All four edges simply supported: w = 0 and zero bending moment normal to each edge.

quiz.q: Why does an in-plane compression increase the deflection a pressure causes?
quiz.a: Once the plate bends, the compressive force on opposite faces of an element points along different slopes and leaves a net normal force in the direction the plate is already bending. It acts like extra pressure, and grows with the deflection, so the effective stiffness falls and vanishes at N<sub>cr</sub>.

quiz.q: For E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33 and t = 5 mm, find D.
In the worked example N<sub>cr</sub> = 25.3 kN/m. If 20 kN/m compression acts, find N<sub>x</sub>/N<sub>cr</sub> and the single-term magnification factor.
In the worked example the single-term magnification predicts 6.71 mm and the full series 6.76 mm. Explain the small difference.
quiz.a: Each Navier term is magnified by its own 1/(1 − N/N<sub>mn</sub>). The first term has the lowest N<sub>mn</sub> and is magnified 1.65 times; the higher terms, which reduce the centre deflection, have much larger N<sub>mn</sub> and are hardly magnified. Their negative share therefore shrinks, so the exact factor is slightly above the single-term value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large-deflection plates need the von Kármán equations, in which the membrane forces depend on w. Finite element plate and shell codes solve the same equations and extract buckling loads from the geometric stiffness matrix. Search for von Kármán plate equations and Levy plate solution.
